summary:
Article 347-1 of Cameroon's penal code criminalises consensual same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, with a maximum sentence of five years' imprisonment. The penal code enacted in 1965 did not criminalise consensual same-sex acts; an ordinance issued in September 1972 by President Ahmadou Ahidjo introduced Article 347bis, now numbered 347-1, and the 2016 penal code restated the prohibition explicitly. Arrests made on grounds of appearance or gender presentation carry sentences of six months to five years.

Law No. 2010/012 of 21 December 2010 on Cybersecurity and Cybercrime creates a separate offence. Article 83(1) punishes sexual propositions to a person of the same sex conveyed through electronic communications with one to two years' imprisonment and a fine of 500,000 to 1,000,000 CFA francs, or either penalty alone; Article 83(2) doubles both where the proposition is followed by sexual intercourse.

Enforcement reaches gender presentation directly. On 8 February 2021 in Douala, two transgender women, Shakiro and Patricia, were arrested in a restaurant for wearing women's clothing and held for five months. They were convicted of attempted homosexuality, public indecency and failing to carry identification, and on 12 May 2021 a Douala court sentenced each to five years' imprisonment, the maximum statutory term, plus a fine of 200,000 CFA francs ($370) each. Their lawyers, Alice Nkom and Richard Tamfu, described the judgment as a political decision with no proof of any act. A judge ordered the pair released until a court could hear their appeals, and an appeal was filed. Shakiro, born 29 July 1997 in Douala, had built a following on Facebook and YouTube discussing trans life, and subsequently fled Cameroon to claim asylum abroad.

Appearance-based convictions predate that case. In November 2011 two young men were jailed for five years solely because they wore women's clothing and ordered a cream-based liqueur; the original judge cited their dress, their speech and the drink as proof they were gay. On 9 January 2013 a Cameroonian appeals court acquitted Jonas Kimie and Franky Ndome. Their lawyer Alice Nkom said the conviction rested on stereotypes with no observed acts, and Amnesty International welcomed the acquittal.

Other documented prosecutions include Jean-Claude Roger Mbede, arrested in 2011 for sending SMS messages to a male acquaintance and sentenced to three years at Kondengui Central Prison; three young men sentenced to five years on 24 November 2011 for oral sex in a parked car; and, in May 2005, eleven men arrested at a nightclub on suspicion of sodomy, against whom the authorities threatened medical examinations to 'prove' homosexual activity. They were detained into February 2006, faced trials scheduled for March 2006 and were released in April 2006.

Human Rights Watch reported on 11 May 2022 that violence against LGBTI people had risen that year: since 9 March 2022 security forces had arbitrarily arrested at least six people and detained eleven, all of them victims of group attacks, over alleged consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity, and gendarmes beat two detainees. A senior researcher at the organisation, Ilaria Allegrozzi, stated that the criminalisation law lets both civilians and security forces abuse LGBTI people without consequence.

The US Department of State's 2010 human rights report recorded harassment and extortion of gays and lesbians by law enforcement and the use of false allegations to harass or extortion, alongside societal discrimination among abuses. A 2020 assessment described Cameroon as prosecuting consensual same-sex conduct more aggressively than almost any country in the world. Reporting in May 2021 placed Cameroon among 31 African countries that criminalise same-sex relations and described beatings of gay and trans people in public as common.

Official hostility has also run through the press. In 2006 tabloids published the names of at least 50 prominent people claimed to be homosexual, which boosted circulation and drew criticism from the state communication council for privacy invasion; President Paul Biya publicly urged respect for privacy while the state continued prosecuting people accused of homosexual activity. On 30 June 2024 the president's daughter, Brenda Biya, came out as a lesbian on Instagram, provoking national backlash and hope among LGBTQ Cameroonians.

Protection machinery is thin. Prisoners accused of homosexuality describe Douala's main prison as 'hell'. Alternatives-Cameroon, an LGBTQ organisation, shut down after a police raid, removing a service base. Few lawyers are willing to defend people accused in homosexuality cases.
tangentialFactors:
Cameroon is one of 31 African countries that criminalise same-sex relations, and a 2020 assessment ranked it among the most aggressive prosecutors of consensual same-sex conduct worldwide. The comparison is one of legal regime, not of measured incident rates: the inventory contains no per-capita or population-adjusted figures for any country, so no ranking of danger can be drawn from it.

The evidentiary standard in appearance-based cases is the recurring turbulence. In the 2011 nightclub case the trial judge treated speech manner, women's clothing and ordering a cream-based liqueur as sufficient proof of homosexuality, a verdict overturned on appeal in January 2013. In the February 2021 case the defence argued there was no proof of any act, and the conviction nonetheless proceeded to the statutory maximum. Failure to carry identification was charged alongside the anti-homosexuality counts, so document irregularity can compound the substantive charge.

Adjacent signals cut in both directions. The 2006 publication of names of at least 50 prominent people drew criticism from the state communication council and a public appeal for privacy from President Biya, while prosecutions continued. The president's daughter's public coming-out on 30 June 2024 produced national backlash alongside expressions of hope among LGBTQ Cameroonians. Neither development altered the statutory position described above.

Outbound asylum material forms a separate strand: in July 2010 the United Kingdom granted a gay Cameroonian man the right to claim asylum, prompting the Minister of Communication, Issa Tchiroma Bakary, to argue that homosexuals are not prosecuted for private activities and that 'he is not the only gay person in Cameroon.' In August 2011 a gay Cameroonian man was granted temporary immigration bail from the UK Border Agency after Air France refused to carry him to Yaoundé, and in May 2012 the same agency sought to return an asylum-seeker it found had produced 'no credible evidence' that he was gay. These are decisions of the receiving state and an airline, not Cameroonian entry or carriage rules.
localsOnly:
Residents face exposure through their online activity as well as in person: Article 83(1) of Law No. 2010/012 reaches same-sex sexual propositions made by electronic communication, carrying one to two years' imprisonment and a fine of 500,000 to 1,000,000 CFA francs, doubled where intercourse follows. Jean-Claude Roger Mbede's 2011 three-year sentence at Kondengui Central Prison arose from SMS messages to a male acquaintance.

Law enforcement conduct toward residents is documented in the 2010 US Department of State report, which recorded harassment and extortion of gays and lesbians by police and the use of false allegations as a means of harassment or extortion. Human Rights Watch recorded arbitrary arrests and detentions by security forces in the period from 9 March 2022, including beatings by gendarmes of two detainees.

Community infrastructure available to residents has been reduced. Alternatives-Cameroon, an LGBTQ organisation, shut down after a police raid. Few lawyers are willing to take homosexuality cases, and the prison where accused men are held is described by prisoners themselves as 'hell'. Residents were also exposed to outing: in 2006 tabloids published the names of at least 50 prominent people claimed to be homosexual.

Residents who leave the country may seek asylum abroad on the strength of these conditions; the record documents a successful UK asylum grant in July 2010 and Shakiro's departure from Cameroon after her 2021 sentence.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Cameroonian visa policy, entry-refusal rule or border-admission procedure for LGBTQ travellers is described in the inventory. The only border-adjacent material concerns outbound decisions by the UK Border Agency and an airline, and a link to UK government travel advice on Cameroonian laws and customs; whether Cameroon applies any screening, questioning or refusal practice at its own ports of entry is unresolved and not sourced.

No information appears on legal gender recognition, name change, or the issuance and amendment of identity documents and gender markers in Cameroon. Whether the identification-failure charge in the February 2021 case reflects a general document-carrying requirement, and how it interacts with any gender-marker question, is not sourced.

Healthcare, HIV services and access to medication for transgender visitors are not described. The health-related material in the inventory is coercive rather than therapeutic: the May 2005 threat of medical examinations to 'prove' homosexual activity among eleven detained men. Whether hormone therapy or other trans-specific care is legally available, restricted or obtainable in Cameroon is unresolved.

No contemporary youth, school or minor-specific legal policy is covered. The only youth-adjacent material is historical ethnography from 1921 concerning a Bafia initiation custom, which carries no present-day legal weight.

The outcome of the appeal in the February 2021 case is unresolved: the sources record that an appeal was filed and that the two women were released pending it, but no appellate judgment is documented. The most recent documented enforcement action in this record is the Human Rights Watch reporting of 11 May 2022 covering arrests from 9 March 2022; no later incident is documented here.
